catalog_citation: Irshied, Omar & Michael Kenstowicz. 1984. Some phonological rules of Bani-Hassan Arabic: a Bedouin dialect. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 14(1): 109-147. Urbana: Dept. of Linguistics, University of Illinois. (archive.org scan studiesinlinguis131411983198…
catalog_locator: pp. 127-129 (section on accent, exx. (46)-(51); secondary-stress footnote c. p. 146 (djvu text, 36050-36090)
catalog_quote: As in Levantine Arabic the major word stress in BHA is located on one of the last three syllables of the word--essentially the rightmost heavy syllable, otherwise the third last. Heavy syllables are those containing a long vowel (CVV) or a short vowel plus consonant (CVC), while light syllables contain a single short vowel CCV). At the stage of the derivation where stress is assigned extraheavy CWC and CVCC are only found in final position, where they naturally also take the major stress. A final CVC syllable counts as light in BHA, as ^n many other languages. If final consonants are ignored in the calculation of syllable weight for the assignment of accent then CVC will count as light while CWC and CVCC will still count as heavy. ... From these data it would appear that BHA has a version of the common Latin stress rule accenting the rightmost heavy syllable and otherwise the antepenult…
sweep_summary: The only title-keyword item, Taine-Cheikh 1988 (BSL 83), was already held by the project (HAL open scan, scanned) and was re-read: it is a syllable/foot/syncope study that marks stress in its transcription (circumflex on stressed long vowels, p. 226 n. 3; examples p. 229) but explicitly defers the stress-placement rules (pp. 249-250) and states no rule. The catalog's deciding source for hass1238, Irshied & Kenstowicz 1984, was downloaded from archive.org and describes Bani-Hassan Arabic, 'a Bedouin dialect of northern Jordan' (Zarqa-Mafraq-Jerash), not Hassaniyya of Mauritania; the mis-attachment comes from WALS code ahs (linked to ISO mey, plotted at 20N 10W) inherited by Glottolog as language code [hass1238]. The best first-hand Hassaniyya statement read is Taine-Cheikh 2007 (EALL II, HAL preprint p. 4): stress on the third mora from the end of the word (mäktäb vs mäktūb), a length accent salient only on long vowels; it should replace the Bani-Hassan quote as the deciding source. classification weight survives (moraic, quantity-sensitive) but the rule text should be corrected from 'rightmost heavy of last three, else antepenult' to 'third mora from the right edge'; the Bani-Hassan quote belongs on a Jordanian Bedouin / South Levantine Arabic record if one exists. Taine-Cheikh 1989/1994 open HAL papers and the 1988 Dictionnaire vol. 1 Introduction (HAL anti-bot block; low priority). for the session was exhausted, so relevance checks used HAL, archive.org, Glottolog and WALS records only.

new_statements.quote: Stress is on the third mora from the end of the word, e.g., on the first syllable in mäktäb 'desk', on the second in mäktūb 'written'. It is strongly marked only on long vowels (accent of length rather than intensity). A lot of grammatical morphemes are clitics.
new_statements.citation: Taine-Cheikh, Catherine. 2007. Ḥassāniyya Arabic. In K. Versteegh et al. (eds.), Encyclopedia of Arabic Language and Linguistics, vol. II, 240-250. Leiden: Brill. (HAL halshs-00563853)
new_statements.locator: §2.1.6 Stress, HAL preprint p. 4 (pdf page 5); printed pp. 240-250
new_statements.reading: Quantity-sensitive stress computed on moras: the syllable containing the third mora from the right edge is stressed — final syllable when it is superheavy (CVVC/CVCC: mäk'tūb, ktâb, debbûs), otherwise the penult (mäk-täb, zrî-be). Phonetically a length accent, salient only on long vowels; clitics join the host's accentual domain. This is a weight-sensitive system, so catalog classification weight stands, but the rule is moraic (third-mora-from-end), not the Levantine 'rightmost heavy of the last three syllables, else antepenult' in the current quote. Taine-Cheikh 1988's stress-marked examples (p. 229: ktâb, ezūzâl, debbûs, zrîbe, ṛaḥḥâle) are consistent with this rule.

sources.note: Explicit first-hand rule for Hassaniyya proper: stress on the syllable containing the third mora from the right edge (so final if the final syllable is superheavy CVVC/CVCC, otherwise penult when the final is CVC or CV); phonetically an accent of length, clearly perceptible only on long vowels. Quantity-sensitive, so compatible with the catalog's classification weight, but the rule is moraic and differs from the Levantine-type 'rightmost heavy of the last three syllables, else antepenult' rule in the catalog quote.
